carrier.title: L1+L2 (dual-frequency)
carrier.body: This station broadcasts on both GPS frequencies — enough for cm-accurate fixes out to ~30 km. L1-only stations work closer in but degrade faster with distance.

carrier-l1.title: L1-only (single-frequency)
carrier-l1.body: This station broadcasts on one GPS frequency. Reliable RTK fixes up to ~10 km; beyond that ionospheric error grows fast and accuracy degrades.

carrier-unknown.title: Accuracy unverified
carrier-unknown.body: This station's sourcetable didn't declare its carrier field — we can't confirm whether it's single- or dual-frequency. It may still work fine; connect and check your receiver's RTK fix quality.

mountpoint.title: Mountpoint
mountpoint.body: The name of the specific correction stream on this caster. You'll paste it into your NTRIP client's 'Mountpoint' or 'Base' field.

whats-this-map.lead: This map shows free public reference stations that broadcast GPS corrections. Connect to one within ~30 km of where you're working and your GPS goes from metres-accurate to centimetres.
whats-this-map.body:
Each coloured dot is one station. The green halos show where its correction is reliable: green <10 km, ~2 cm · lime 10–30 km, centimetre-level · amber 30–50 km, accuracy grows with distance · red 50–100 km, decimetre range.

Click any dot to get connection details — server, port, mountpoint, and credentials — to enter into your receiver or phone app.
whats-this-map.deep: Purple rings are VRS (virtual networks — one connection point, the network picks a base for you). Grey rings are networks that exist but aren't yet ingested into this feed. Circled ? marks paid or restricted networks, shown for reference only.

is-my-gear-compatible.lead: You need a dedicated dual-frequency (L1+L2) GNSS receiver — almost all phones and consumer GPS devices can't do RTK in real-time, and purpose-built units start around €275.
is-my-gear-compatible.body:
How to check:

  1. Look in the receiver's datasheet for L1+L2, dual-band, or dual-frequency.
  2. Or look for an NTRIP, Network RTK, or Internet RTK option in the receiver's settings menu. If it's there, you're compatible.

Most professional surveying equipment from Trimble, Leica, Topcon, Sokkia, South and Hi-Target made in the past ~15 years supports this.
is-my-gear-compatible.deep: L5 is a third frequency — nice but not required. Triple-band receivers perform better under tree cover and converge faster. The hobbyist sweet spot is dual-band u-blox ZED-F9P (ArduSimple, SparkFun RTK, Emlid Reach RS2+).

what-to-buy.q: I don't have gear yet — what should I buy?
what-to-buy.lead: For free network RTK, ready-to-use kits start around €449 / $490. DIY tinkerer kits from ~€275. You don't need the €2,900+ standalone category unless you work somewhere with no mobile signal.
what-to-buy.body:
Four paths:

  • DIY — ArduSimple simpleRTK2B kit (~€275). Requires more setup; standard choice for building your own base station too.
  • Ready-to-use hobbyist — ArduSimple RTK Handheld 2 Kit (~€449 / $490). Compact, battery included, Bluetooth. Android-preferred (iOS: SW Maps only).
  • All-in-one rover — SparkFun RTK Facet (~$739). NTRIP client built in; connects via Bluetooth. Android-preferred (iOS: SW Maps only). Available from Mouser, Digi-Key, and SparkFun directly.
  • Survey-grade — Emlid Reach RS2+ (~$2,200) or RS3 (~$3,000). Rugged, waterproof, one-click NTRIP in Emlid Flow. Full iOS support.
what-to-buy.deep:
Avoid anything sold as 'survey-grade' that doesn't explicitly list L1+L2 or NTRIP — it's usually SBAS/DGPS-grade and gets you sub-metre at best. Subscription-dependent hardware (from ~$850) like Trimble Catalyst DA2 needs paid correction fees on top and typically won't work with the free networks this map shows.

If you need centimetre accuracy with no mobile signal at all, look at standalone PPP receivers — Galileo HAS-capable units start around €2,700 / $2,900 with no ongoing fees. Search 'Galileo HAS receiver' or 'PPP receiver' to explore that category. This map is not about those.

how-to-connect-emlid.q: How do I connect this station in my app?
how-to-connect-emlid.sub: Emlid Flow · SW Maps · other NTRIP clients
how-to-connect-emlid.lead: Open your NTRIP client's 'correction input' or 'NTRIP' settings, paste the values from the station popup, and press Connect.
how-to-connect-emlid.body:
Fields every NTRIP client asks for, mapped to the popup:

  • Host / Caster address → Server (e.g. crtk.net)
  • Port → Port (use the value shown in the popup)
  • Mountpoint → Mount (e.g. AMPH)
  • Username / Password → from the popup. For open sources, a generic user/pass is shown — paste it directly. Sources requiring registration use your account credentials.

Once connected, your receiver needs a few seconds to reach "RTK fix." If it sticks at "float," your baseline is too long — pick a closer station.
how-to-connect-emlid.deep:
App-specific tips:

Emlid Flow: Settings → NTRIP → Add caster. Leave 'Receive GGA' on for VRS/NEAR mountpoints.
SW Maps: Connection settings → External NTRIP Caster. SW Maps can forward corrections to bluetooth receivers.
u-center: Receiver → NTRIP Client. Remember to enable UBX-RXM-RTCM output if you want to verify fix quality.

near-mountpoint.lead: Some networks (Centipede, rtk2go) publish a special mountpoint called NEAR. Connect to it and the caster automatically sends corrections from whichever base is closest to you.
near-mountpoint.body:
Use NEAR when:

  • You're mobile and crossing station boundaries.
  • You don't want to hardcode one station name and forget it's offline.

Your NTRIP client must send a GGA sentence (its current position) back to the caster, otherwise NEAR has nothing to go on. Most clients do this by default.

NEAR doesn't appear as a pin on this map — type it directly into your NTRIP client's mountpoint field.
near-mountpoint.deep: NEAR isn't part of the NTRIP spec — it's a caster-side convention. Centipede, rtk2go and a few others implement it. If you paste 'NEAR' on a network that doesn't support it, you'll get a 404 or silent no-corrections.

vrs-explained.lead: A VRS network synthesises a virtual reference station at your location, using real stations around you. One connection point, uniform cm-accuracy anywhere inside the coverage.
vrs-explained.body:
Purple rings on the map mark VRS networks. You connect once and never have to switch stations as you move.

Your app needs to send your current position to the network — look for a 'send GGA', 'send NMEA position', or 'Receive GGA' toggle and make sure it's on. Most apps enable this by default.
vrs-explained.deep: Under the hood, the network runs a network-RTK solver (most commonly Trimble VRS or a Geo++ MAC equivalent) that models atmosphere from 3+ neighbouring bases. For users, the practical difference vs a single base is: (a) no baseline-distance penalty, (b) no station picking, (c) slightly longer time-to-first-fix on connection.

carrier-l1l2.q: L1+L2 vs L1-only — what does it mean?
carrier-l1l2.lead: Your receiver tracks signals on two radio frequency bands. Using both lets it measure and remove ionospheric delay — the main error that grows with distance — extending reliable RTK from ~10 km out to ~30 km.
carrier-l1l2.body:
Rough rule of thumb:

  • L1+L2 (dual-frequency) — 1–3 cm within 10 km of a station; typically better than 5 cm within 30 km.
  • L1-only — centimetre-level within ~10 km, but degrades fast beyond that and is much more ionosphere-sensitive.

If a station is marked "Accuracy unverified" on this map, its sourcetable didn't declare the carrier field — doesn't mean it's bad, just that we can't confirm it.
carrier-l1l2.deep: Modern receivers use L1+L2+L5 (triple-band) for fastest convergence and best multipath rejection under canopy. For plain-open-sky work, dual-band is fine.

float-vs-fix.q: Why is my receiver stuck in 'float'?
float-vs-fix.lead: Float means your receiver is using corrections but hasn't resolved the carrier-phase ambiguities. Accuracy is ~decimetre, not centimetre. Common causes: baseline too long, poor sky view, weak correction stream.
float-vs-fix.body:
1. Check the baseline — is the station within 30 km? Further out, float is normal.
  2. Clear sky view? Trees and buildings block low-elevation satellites you need for ambiguity resolution.
  3. Check your NTRIP client shows incoming bytes / RTCM messages. No data means the caster connection is dead.
  4. Give it 60 seconds of clear sky. Fix can take 30–90 s on cold start.
float-vs-fix.deep: In L1-only RTK, fix may never be achievable beyond ~15 km. In L1+L2, expect fix out to 30–40 km under good conditions. Legacy RTCM 2.x streams carry less information — modern receivers increasingly don't accept them; the popup warns when a station is 2.x only.

mountpoint.sub: The address of one correction stream
mountpoint.lead: A mountpoint is the name of the specific station you're connecting to — it's what you type into the 'Mountpoint', 'Stream', or 'Base name' field in your app.
mountpoint.body: When you click a pin on this map, the Mount value in the popup is exactly what goes in your app. One server can host hundreds of stations, each with its own mountpoint name.
mountpoint.deep: Sourcetables (the caster's listing of mountpoints) follow RTCM spec 10402.1. Each entry declares: stream name, location, carrier, messages, auth. This map's data pipeline parses sourcetables 4× daily to build the pin list.

legacy-rtcm.lead: RTCM 2.x is the 1990s-era correction message format. Many modern receivers — including consumer-grade F9P boards — no longer decode it reliably. We flag these streams so you don't waste an afternoon debugging.
legacy-rtcm.body: Most free networks now broadcast RTCM 3.x (messages 1005, 1074, 1084, 1094 etc.). If the popup shows the legacy warning, try another station first.
legacy-rtcm.deep: Some older Trimble / Topcon hardware still prefers RTCM 2.x — if you own equipment from that era, the legacy streams might actually be what you want.

build-base.q: Can I set up my own base station?
build-base.sub: If the map shows no coverage near you
build-base.lead: Yes. A second RTK receiver at a fixed surveyed point broadcasts corrections through a free caster; your rover connects to it like any other station on this map.
build-base.body:
• Hardware: any dual-frequency RTK receiver (the ArduSimple simpleRTK2B starter kit works well), power, internet
  • Software: RTKBase — open-source, runs on a Raspberry Pi, web interface
  • Caster: Centipede and/or RTK2Go — free public NTRIP casters; register your base and it becomes accessible from anywhere
build-base.deep:
Honest effort: first setup takes a weekend if you're comfortable with Linux and basic networking. Additional hardware cost roughly €200–450 depending on what you already have.

For a properly accurate base: stable antenna mount with ground plane, clear 360° sky view, position surveyed by PPP (24h minimum, a week is better). An improvised roof-mount is fine for experimenting but won't produce centimetre-accurate corrections.

access-tiers.q: Open / Registration / Conditions — what's the difference?
access-tiers.lead: All stations on this map are free. The tier labels tell you what paperwork you need first.
access-tiers.body:
• Open — no signup. Paste credentials (often a generic user/pass) and connect.
  • Registration — free account, usually approved instantly or in 1–2 days. An email and a form.
  • Conditions — free only for specific users (e.g. non-commercial, agricultural) or within a defined trial period. Check the network's site for current terms.
access-tiers.deep: The 'Restricted' tier (circled ? pins) is a separate category — paid or identity-gated networks shown on the map for reference only. They're not usable via this site's data.

can-i-share.q: Can I share a link to a specific station?
can-i-share.lead: Yes — the URL updates as you pan, zoom, or select a pin. Copy the address bar to share a view; the recipient opens it and lands on the same centre, zoom and selected mountpoint.
can-i-share.body: Just copy from the address bar — no extra steps needed.
